statement: After the break the lecture covers how Amazon uses a central ID generation service, then Flickr, Twitter, Instagram and pagination; pagination is presented as a very interesting side effect of having a good ID generation system.
detail: The teacher also promises a demo of why people choose one approach over another and how to make those trade-off decisions.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: And we'll talk about Amazon, Flickr, Twitter, Instagram, and pagination. A very interesting side effect of having a good ID generation system.

statement: The teacher knows how Amazon generates IDs because the team that built it sat right next to him; he attended their tech talks, asked them questions, and they explained it in a public tech talk.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I know this because the team that did it sat right next to me, so I used to attend a bunch of tech talks there.

statement: Amazon assigns a globally unique ID to every order placed; the same ID service, built for high throughput, also provides IDs to many other internal services, orders being just one of them.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: for every order that you place is, they assign a global ID to that order, and that is unique.

statement: Amazon's ID service leverages batching; batching is one of the most effective ways to get performance out of any system.
detail: The exact wording of the general claim is partly lost in the transcript ('Batching is one of the most ... performance out of any system').
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you leverage batching.

statement: The Amazon-style ID generation service is simple enough to write in about 150 lines of Python; scaling it only needs a few extra cases handled. The teacher recommends writing it yourself.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You can literally write this thing in 150 lines of code, not even exaggerated.

statement: Architecture of Amazon's ID service: basic API servers exposing ID generation endpoints, put behind a load balancer, backed by a database.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: they use a basic API server exposing your ID generation endpoints, putting behind a load balancer, classic thing, and have a database.

statement: The database behind the ID service is a classic relational database; no fancy non-relational database is needed, and the teacher prefers not to complicate things.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now this database is a classic relational database. No fancy non-relational database.

statement: Core idea of Amazon's approach: instead of calling the remote ID service every time an ID is needed, a server gets a batch of IDs in one shot - the same idea as writing the counter to disk once every thousand IDs instead of on every ID.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: instead of calling your remote service every time you need an ID, you get a batch of IDs in one shot. That's the core idea.

statement: There are YouTube videos on this design, but the lecture goes into its implementation details; having covered the airline check-in system earlier, this design becomes a piece of cake.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Given that we covered airline check-in system, this becomes a piece of cake.

statement: Example setup: two services, orders and payments, each running on its own set of servers, obtain IDs from the central service; they do not care about monotonicity, they only need uniqueness.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: They don't care about monotonicity, FYI. They don't care about monotonicity. They need uniqueness, as simple as that.

statement: When an order-service server boots up it asks the ID service for, e.g., 500 IDs; the API server fires a SQL query on the table, updates the stored value to 500 and sends back the range 0-500.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Hey, I just booted up. Can you give me 500 IDs?

statement: The ID service sends only the start and end of the range, not individual IDs: they are just integers, so there is no need to send so much data over the network.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You don't have to send individual IDs. No, start and end.

statement: The range allocation is done atomically: select the current value FOR UPDATE inside a transaction and update the final handed-over value, so multiple concurrent requests for the same service do not interfere.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You would do it for update, like select start from this for update, do it in a transaction

statement: Walkthrough: server 1 boots with no IDs and gets 0-500 (stored value updated to 500); server 2 boots, the value is incremented by 500 to 1000, and it gets 500-1000.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So it sends 500 to 1000 in response over here.

statement: Order-service servers keep their range in memory; when external order requests arrive they pull IDs from that in-memory range and write into their own orders database without worrying about anything; these become globally unique IDs, optionally prefixed per the service's conventions.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: because they already have the range of IDs in memory, they can start pulling that out.

statement: The central ID generation service decouples the system: because ID generation is separate from the orders database, the orders database can be sharded and scaled horizontally with every shard accepting writes, and servers do not call the ID service for every ID.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: this central ID generation service just decouples the system.

statement: 500 IDs per batch is only a small example; in reality batches are 10,000, 50,000 or 100,000 IDs depending on the service's throughput.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I use 500 as a small example. In reality it is 10,000, 50,000, 100,000, and depending on the throughput of the service

statement: Batch size trade-off: if a server crashes after receiving a range, that range is lost; too small a batch means too-frequent network calls, too large a batch means losing a big range on a crash. Each service tunes the max batch size to its throughput.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If it is too large and if your server crashes, you are losing that entire range.

statement: The ID table holds one entry (row) per service - one for orders, one for payments - so each service's IDs come from its own counter.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Similarly, you had one entry for orders. Similarly, you would have one entry for payment service.

statement: A server loads a range once and refills when it is about to be exhausted: e.g. with 490 of 500 used it calls the service for another 500 and might get 3000-3500, then continues from that range.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: let's say it got 500, 490 are already exhausted, what it would do, it would make call and get another 500.

statement: The batched-range approach does not guarantee monotonicity across servers; it only hands out unique IDs in batches.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So we are still not guaranteeing monotonicity across servers, but you are handing them those IDs in batches.

statement: Implementing the range allocation is the airline check-in system pattern copied over: in a transaction read the value, atomically add the requested count, and return the old and new values as the range.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Airline check-in system, Ctrl-C, Ctrl-V over here.

statement: Amazon's approach is really simple to build: the database is a single source of truth on a single server, so there is no gossip with anyone; it scales easily because each request is just one tiny update, not even a full read.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: here, the single source of truth, because this is single server, it doesn't have to gossip with anyone.

statement: A student proposed tracking in a database how much of its range each server has used, so that on restart the server resumes from there and IDs are not wasted (e.g. with 10,000-ID batches and 100 used, 9,900 are lost forever).
detail: The teacher rejected it: keeping track of every single used ID is a massive overhead, and the ID space (big integer, 2^64) is so large it will never be exhausted; the student accepted this as fine for practical use.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: I was wondering why was that a database not used to keep track of information, how much out of range a server has used

statement: Tracking every used ID to avoid wasting ranges is a massive overhead and not worth it, because a big-integer (2^64) ID space will never be exhausted, even by Amazon.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Imagine the overhead that you would have to keep in, in order to keep track of every single one of them. That's a massive overhead.

statement: Think about practicality at every step: no one cares about using every single ID; it is just a few ranges of numbers lost.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: think about practicality at every step.

statement: People tend to underestimate numbers: 1 million and 1 billion are both huge, and the difference between a million and a billion is itself almost a billion.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: The difference between a million and a billion is almost equal to a billion, and that's huge.

statement: A four-byte integer gives about 4 billion IDs - 4 billion Amazon orders; if even that is exhausted, moving to 64 bits gives a range big enough not to worry about.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Imagine 4 billion orders of Amazon.

statement: A student asked: if monotonicity is not a requirement, why not just use UUIDs? The teacher takes this up as the question of why companies at scale do not prefer UUIDs.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: if monotonicity was not a requirement, then why not just go ahead with a UUID kind of approach?
flags: check: speaker of the UUID question (Student?)

statement: Companies at scale do not prefer UUIDs because they are extremely inefficient at scale.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: They are extremely inefficient at scale.

statement: UUIDs are 128-bit values - 128-bit strings that can be represented as gigantic integers.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: UUIDs are 128 bit integers. Integers as it, 128 bit strings, which can be represented as gigantic integers.

statement: If your company uses UUIDs, then yes, it is inefficient at scale.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: are we inefficient at scale? Yes, you are.
flags: check: teacher voicing a hypothetical student question, or a real student?

statement: The second-week pre-reads included a video on how indexes make database reads faster.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: in the second week pre-reads, I shared a video on how indexes make database read faster.

statement: Database indexes are themselves just tables (effectively B+ trees) holding the indexed values and the IDs of the rows they point to; they are managed internally by the database.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: indexes are also just tables with indexed values and the IDs of the rows that it points to.

statement: For a post table with user ID, post ID, title etc., an index on user ID is effectively a new table with just two columns: the post's user ID and the post ID.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If you are creating an index on user ID, it is effectively a new B+ tree or a new table

statement: In a dense index every index row also stores the row ID, so a big ID type makes the index bulky.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: because in index for a dense index at every single row of your database or of your index, they are also storing the row ID.

statement: A 128-bit UUID is 16 bytes versus a 4-byte integer ID, so switching to UUIDs bloats the index by a factor of four: a 1 GB index becomes 4 GB.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So your index, which was one GB in size is now suddenly four GB in size.

statement: To get maximum performance a database must fit all its indexes in RAM; if they do not fit, no amount of other optimization will make it fast.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It should be able to fit all the indexes in RAM.

statement: How a query executes (in any database with indexes): it first builds a query execution plan, doing all operations on the small indexes - e.g. a join of two tables on indexed columns can be done in memory - and only as the last step goes to disk to read the full rows of the result.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Once it knows the result, then it goes to the disk and reads the entire row. So that's the last step.

statement: If the indexes are in RAM, the entire query execution happens in RAM and only the result rows are read from disk, making execution lightning fast.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So if your indexes are in RAM, entire query execution happens in RAM.

statement: When someone tells the teacher their database is slow, the first thing he checks is index sizes: in most cases they are the problem (random indexes created on the database), and he sees indexes spilling to disk, so reading them requires disk access and is very slow.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: The first thing I do is check their index sizes. That's it. When most cases index sizes are the problem.

statement: A database does not permanently hold indexes in RAM - disk is the main source - but it loads them into RAM during boot-up or when a query needs them, and keeps them there.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it loads it in RAM during boot up or whenever you are requesting it to

statement: The RAM of the database server should be equal to or more than the total index size; otherwise query execution is pathetically slow.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So the RAM of your database server should be equal to, or should be more than what your total index size is.

statement: Later case studies show designs where people did not use UUIDs because of this index-size problem.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I'll tell you other designs where because of this, people have not used UUIDs.

statement: UUIDs, being gigantic 16-byte integers (4x larger), do not index well and bloat up the index.
detail: The teacher closes the UUID discussion with 'In most cases they would get four of them. So which is why people don't use UUIDs.' - the first sentence is unclear.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So they do not index well and they bloat up the index.
flags: check: "get four of them" - go for them?

statement: UUIDs are good for security: they look random and the next one cannot be predicted, so it is hard for anyone to predict other IDs or scrape the whole website.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But they're good for security because you cannot predict what's next in terms of UUID.

statement: If you build Facebook and expose sequential database IDs (1, 2, 3, ...), anyone can fire REST requests in a loop from 0 to 1 billion and scrape the entire website.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: people can just fire REST requests and start from for I equal to zero, I is less than 1 billion I plus plus

statement: UUIDs are not forbidden: if the application is small and will never hit that scale, UUIDs are just fine. Do not unnecessarily go for the best solution; see what works best for you.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Don't unnecessarily go for the best solution out there. See what works for you the best.

statement: MongoDB IDs are 12-byte (96-bit) values: the first 4 bytes are epoch time (always first), then 5 random bytes, then a 3-byte counter.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So MongoDB IDs are 12 byte integers.

statement: MongoDB chose 12 bytes rather than the 16 bytes of a UUID; nothing stopped them from using UUIDs, they went smaller to save four bytes.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: They didn't go for 16 for UUID.

statement: MySQL auto-increment IDs are 4-byte integers, giving a very tiny index; 4 or 8 bytes is still doable, but beyond 8 bytes you should worry about performance at scale.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Four bytes, eight bytes is still doable beyond eight bytes. You should worry about the performance at scale, at scale.

statement: A recurring pattern in ID generation schemes is putting time on the left side and keeping the ID small; this is why IDs growing longer was a problem in the first-half brainstorming - long IDs do not index well.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: like having time on the left side and trying to keep the ID smaller

statement: Every one of the further case studies in the lecture mentions not choosing UUIDs because they do not index well.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: every single one of the further case studies mentioned that they didn't go for UUIDs because they do not index well.

statement: Flickr was the pre-Instagram photo platform (the 'Instagram of the 2010s'), where a lot got posted before Instagram took over.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Flickr was Instagram of 2010s to 2010s.

statement: Flickr needed a central ID generation service because its database was sharded and operated in multi-master mode, so writes could go anywhere; using auto-increment on every shard would produce conflicting IDs.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: they cannot just use auto increment everywhere because that would result to conflict.

statement: Flickr's blog explains they did not use UUIDs because UUIDs index badly.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: And in their blog, they mentioned why not UUIDs? Because they index badly.

statement: The '16 bytes makes the index 4x' figure is a rough estimate (don't quote it): the 4x calculation is not exactly right and actually depends on the values.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Almost rough estimate. Don't quote me on that because your integer was 4 bytes.

statement: Flickr's official blog states that if you cannot fit indexes in memory you cannot make your database fast, and the teacher agrees this is true.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: this is what it's written in their blog, their official blog: if you cannot fit indexes in memory you cannot make your database

statement: Whenever a senior engineer, technical architect or principal engineer optimizes a database, the first thing they look at is index size: if the index has spilled to disk the database will always be slow.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the first thing he or she looks at is the index size. Always remember this.

statement: Provisioning heuristic for the real world (not interviews, which the teacher calls crappy): the database's memory must be at bare minimum the sum of the sizes of all the indexes it holds; anything beyond that is good.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: should be the summation of sizes of all the indexes that it holds. Simple. Bare minimum.

statement: The database is the most essential but most brutal component of an infrastructure: API servers and most other things are stateless and easy to scale, while the database stores everything, is queried for everything, and handles the entire load.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: database is the most brutal component of the most essential, but most brutal component of an infrastructure because scaling API servers is easy.

statement: Database fundamentals are very important: understand whichever database you use really well.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So understand your database, whichever database you are using really well.

statement: Flickr built a central 'ticket server' - an ID generation service - on top of MySQL: whoever needs an ID makes a query to MySQL and gets one.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So Flickr built a central ticket server, basically ID generation service. And they built it on top of MySQL.

statement: When studying another company's design, focus on the beauty of the design and pick its good parts rather than pointing out faults (e.g. performance of querying MySQL per ID) - it was their decision.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: As an engineer, focus on the beauty of design rather than pointing out the faults.

statement: Critiquing another company's design choices is like neighbours fighting: you may know both are wrong, but it is their life; let them do it and pick the best parts.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It's like your neighbors are fighting. You know that both of them are wrong, but you should not say anything to them.

statement: Flickr's 'tickets' table has a column id (BIGINT, unsigned, NOT NULL, AUTO_INCREMENT, the primary key - big integer means a 2^64 space) and a column stub with a unique key.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: they created a table called tickets. In this table, they added a column called id, big integer, unsigned, not null and auto increment.

statement: Flickr's idea: if MySQL already gives auto-increment IDs, MySQL itself can be the ID generation service - answering an earlier student question about using the database as the ID generator.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: The idea is that if MySQL already gives me auto increment ids, why can't MySQL be my id generation service?

statement: Flickr's ID-generation database is separate from the sharded photos database; it only leverages the database's auto-increment to generate IDs.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: your ID generation itself is a separate database in which you are leveraging the auto-incrementedness of the database as your ID generation.

statement: Naive way to use a database as an ID generator: whenever an ID is needed, delete the row and insert a new one; the auto-increment column gives the next ID each time.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You would delete this and add a new row. When you add a new row, what would you get? It would be the next ID.

statement: The stub column exists only because you cannot insert a row with no values; it is a normal dummy column holding a dummy value, nothing special despite the fancy name.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It's a normal column, name seems fancy, just a normal dummy column, some dummy value, nothing special about it

statement: Delete-and-insert can be done in one transaction, or replaced by an upsert, since delete plus insert equals upsert.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: either we delete or increment, delete and insert in one transaction, or we can use upsert, because delete plus insert is equal to upsert

statement: Upsert: try to insert something; if it already exists, update it; if it does not exist, insert it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You're trying to insert something. If it exists, then update. If it does not exist, then insert.

statement: MySQL's INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE tries to insert the given values and, if that fails due to a unique key constraint, runs the update you passed - a classic upsert.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But if it fails due to unique key constraint, then it triggers the update that you pass it.

statement: MySQL's second upsert option is REPLACE INTO (analogous to INSERT INTO, seen earlier in the key-value store on a relational database); internally it deletes the row and inserts a new one.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: what replaceInto does internally, it actually deletes and inserts the new row.

statement: REPLACE INTO is about 32x slower than INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE; the teacher personally benchmarked this on a MySQL server. Either works - what matters is doing an upsert.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: replace into is 32 times slower than this. I personally benchmarked this.

statement: Flickr's ID query: INSERT INTO tickets (stub) VALUES ('a') ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE id = id + 1, with a constant stub value; the insert hits the existing 'a', so the update bumps the id (e.g. 74 to 75) and returns it; subsequent queries give 76, 77, 78 and so on.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: insert into ticket stub a on duplicate key update ID equal to ID plus one. Simple.

statement: Flickr's approach leverages MySQL's transactions and atomicity to produce IDs.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You are leveraging MySQL transaction, MySQL atomicity in order to get the IDs that you want.

statement: Flickr request flow: a post-photo request reaches a photo-service API server, which fires a request to the separate MySQL ID server to get an ID and then stores the photo in the sharded photos database.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: API server fires the request to this MySQL to get the ID. You get the ID, then you store it in photos.

statement: A single MySQL ID server is a single point of failure: if that one server goes down, ID generation is gone.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: this is a single point of failure, because there is one server. If this server goes down, then gone.

statement: The fix is two ID database servers behind a load balancer, so if one goes down the other handles the load; this resembles the earlier gossip/monotonicity problem, but here monotonicity is not needed. A student had recommended this approach earlier.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So what we do, we put both databases behind a load balancer and make one, someone also recommended this approach.

statement: Uniqueness across the two servers is ensured by incrementing by 2 instead of 1: one database generates odd IDs, the other even IDs.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: instead of doing increment plus plus, I do increment plus equal to two. Let's say one database generates odd IDs, other database generates even IDs.

statement: This is configured with MySQL server settings auto_increment_increment (how much to increment each time, set to 2) and auto_increment_offset (the starting point, set to 1).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Auto increment increment is set to 2 and auto increment offset is set to 1.

statement: With the load balancer in round-robin mode, requests alternate between servers and get IDs 1, 2, 3, 4, ... in turn, so the IDs come out almost monotonic.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So first request goes over here. It generates ID 1. Second request goes to other server.
flags: unclear: "positive request 2 year, 2nd year, 3rd year 4th year, 5th year, 6th year, 7th year, 8th year"

statement: Two servers solve the single point of failure: if one goes down, ID generation continues without hiccups.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You have solved problem of single point of failure.

statement: If the odd server dies (say after generating 5) all requests go to the even server (2, 4, 6, ...); if it comes back after 202 was generated, it resumes where it left off because MySQL is persistent, giving 7, 204, 9, 206, 11, 208 - a huge discrepancy that is a matter of aesthetics, not correctness; IDs stay unique.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It just does not look aesthetically pleasing. Much more for aesthetics rather than correctness.

statement: Optional fix when a server comes back: take the max generated ID (e.g. 202), add a buffer (e.g. to 240), and reset the servers to 241 and 242 so they resume 242, 243, 244, ...
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Let's say this generated ID to 202. You will add some buffer, let's say 240, and you set here 241 and 242.

statement: The max-plus-buffer reset is purely for aesthetics, not correctness; strict monotonicity is still not guaranteed, but nearly monotonic IDs are a good byproduct to have.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It's just for aesthetics, nothing about correctness, nothing about strict monotonicity.

statement: Flickr's ticket-server approach is pretty simple but pretty brilliant in its own sense.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It's pretty simple, but it's pretty brilliant in its own sense.

statement: Who resets the servers: when a database server goes down it is a big deal and an SRE/DevOps engineer looks into it and reconfigures; alternatively automate it: find the active server, find the max IDs, add a buffer, set the values, and do a quick process reboot on each server.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: find the active server, find the max IDs, add some buffer to that, and then set the values
flags: unclear: "Ordin event and results back up."

statement: Asked how the ticket query yields a unique value: the insert (with no id given) of the same stub value fails because stub has a unique key, so ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE runs id = id + 1.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But stub is having what? Unique key. Correct? What would happen? This insert would fail.

statement: The stub value is just a hard-coded constant in the query (literally any string); its only purpose is to make the database break the unique constraint so the update fires atomically - there is no other reason for stub.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You are making your database break the unique constraint so that you can trigger an update atomic.

statement: Asked how the buffered reset is done: an engineer does it; the configuration is MySQL-specific (look up how to change auto_increment_offset), and it is only for aesthetics - the system keeps running correctly without it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This configuration, these configurations, it's MySQL specific. Check how you can change auto increment offset on the platform.

statement: Worked through with a student: odd server died at 5 while the even server reached 202; when the odd server returns it would generate 7 while the even one generates 204. Resetting both sides only makes it look better; without it the system still functions correctly.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Even if you don't do it, your system would still function correctly.

statement: What value to reset to is the architect's choice - e.g. start with 240 and 239 and let round robin continue; reset to the safest value, which is why the safest value was discussed earlier (starting safely beyond IDs generated in the past).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You reset it to the safest value of that.

statement: A student argued that without the max-plus-buffer reset the odd server restarting at 7 would make IDs not monotonically increasing; the teacher replied that monotonicity was never enforced here - it is only a nice byproduct.
detail: Corrected by the teacher: 'Where did we enforce monotonicity?'; the student agreed it is never enforced here.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: the odd server starts producing IDs from let's say seven, then they are not monotonically increasing.
flags: check: "let's add five" - "let's say at five"?

statement: Not everyone needs monotonic IDs and it is okay not to have them - e.g. social media has no reason to care about monotonicity.
detail: The teacher's final words 'You should have it.' are ambiguous in context.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Not everyone needs monotonicity. And it's okay to not have it.
flags: check: "You should have it." - meaning unclear
